verses.text: Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Becorath, the son of Aphiah, the son of a Benjamite, a mighty man of valor.
He had a son, whose name was Saul, an impressive young man; and there was not among the children of Israel a better person than he. From his shoulders and upward he was taller than any of the people.
The donkeys of Kish, Saul’s father, were lost. Kish said to Saul his son, “Take now one of the servants with you, and arise, go look for the donkeys.”

He passed through the hill country of Ephraim, and passed through the land of Shalishah, but they didn’t find them. Then they passed through the land of Shaalim, and there they weren’t there. Then he passed through the land of the Benjamites, but they didn’t find them.
When they had come to the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant who was with him, “Come, and let us return, lest my father stop caring about the donkeys, and be anxious for us.”

The servant said to him, “Behold now, there is in this city a man of God, and he is a man who is held in honor. All that he says surely happens. Now let us go there. Perhaps he can tell us which way to go.”
Then Saul said to his servant, “But, behold, if we go, what should we bring the man? For the bread is spent in our sacks, and there is not a present to bring to the man of God. What do we have?”
The servant answered Saul again, and said, “Behold, I have in my hand the fourth part of a shekel  of silver. I will give that to the man of God, to tell us our way.”
(In earlier times in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he said, “Come, and let us go to the seer”; for he who is now called a prophet was before called a seer.)
Then Saul said to his servant, “Well said. Come, let us go.” So they went to the city where the man of God was.
As they went up the ascent to the city, they found young maidens going out to draw water, and said to them, “Is the seer here?”
They answered them, and said, “He is. Behold, he is before you. Hurry now, for he has come today into the city; for the people have a sacrifice today in the high place.

As soon as you have come into the city, you will immediately find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat; for the people will not eat until he come, because he blesses the sacrifice. Afterwards those who are invited eat. Now therefore go up; for at this time you will find him.”
They went up to the city. As they came within the city, behold, Samuel came out toward them, to go up to the high place.
Now Yahweh had revealed to Samuel a day before Saul came, saying,

“Tomorrow about this time I will send you a man out of the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him to be prince over my people Israel. He will save my people out of the hand of the Philistines; for I have looked upon my people, because their cry has come to me.”
When Samuel saw Saul, Yahweh said to him, “Behold, the man of whom I spoke to you! He will have authority over my people.”
Then Saul approached Samuel in the gateway, and said, “Please tell me where the seer’s house is.”
Samuel answered Saul, and said, “I am the seer. Go up before me to the high place, for you are to eat with me today. In the morning I will let you go, and will tell you all that is in your heart.

As for your donkeys who were lost three days ago, don’t set your mind on them; for they have been found. For whom is all that is desirable in Israel? Is it not for you, and for all your father’s house?”
Saul answered, “Am I not a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? And my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then do you speak to me like this?”
Samuel took Saul and his servant, and brought them into the guest room, and made them sit in the best place among those who were invited, who were about thirty persons.
Samuel said to the cook, “Bring the portion which I gave you, of which I said to you, ‘Set it aside.’”

The cook took up the thigh, and that which was on it, and set it before Saul. Samuel said, “Behold, that which has been reserved! Set it before yourself and eat; because for the appointed time has it been kept for you, for I said, ‘I have invited the people.’” So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
When they had come down from the high place into the city, he talked with Saul on the housetop.
They arose early; and about daybreak, Samuel called to Saul on the housetop, saying, “Get up, that I may send you away.” Saul arose, and they both went outside, he and Samuel, together.

As they were going down at the end of the city, Samuel said to Saul, “Tell the servant to go on ahead of us.” He went ahead, then Samuel said, “But stand still first, that I may cause you to hear God’s message.”

footnotes.content: Kish's line stretches back five generations—a man of Benjamin known for valor. I wonder if Kish ever imagined his quiet faithfulness would be the ground from which a king would grow. Sometimes the Lord builds kingdoms not from the proud but from those who tend their flocks faithfully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul stands head and shoulders above the crowd—impressive, young, better than anyone around him. The text seems almost breathless describing him. Yet how often have I seen the best outward form hide the most fragile heart. The Lord would later teach Saul what heights and strengths cannot do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lost donkeys—such a small thing. Yet I notice how the Lord often moves through small losses to redirect us toward something we didn't know we needed. Saul sets out hunting for animals; he returns anointed as king. The Father wastes nothing, not even our inconveniences.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ephraim, Shalishah, Shaalim, the land of the Benjamites—a long search through familiar territory where nothing is found. How well I know that feeling of covering ground without result. But the Lord sees farther than our seeking eyes. Every mile they walked was carrying Saul toward his true appointment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul worries now—not about the donkeys but about his father's heart. He feels the weight of his father's anxiety, wants to ease it. There is something tender here: a son concerned for his father's peace. The Lord sees that tenderness and honors it by drawing him near.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servant speaks up—practical, hopeful. "All that he says surely happens." That is Samuel's name, his calling: he speaks what God says, and it comes to pass. Even servants know a true prophet by his fruit. How grateful I am when someone near us speaks truth that reshapes our path.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul hesitates—practical and humble. They have nothing to bring, no gift worthy of a man of God. His concern shows he understands something sacred is needed here, not mere commerce. Sometimes our poverty is what makes us ready to receive what grace alone can give.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A quarter shekel—little silver, carefully kept in hand. The servant offers what he has, nothing grand. I've always loved that the Lord honors such offerings. A widow's mite, a servant's quarter shekel—these are the currency of heaven, pressed forward by faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The text pauses to explain the old name: seer, now called prophet. Words change, but the office remains—men and women who see what the Lord shows and speak it forth. Every generation needs voices willing to look past what others see and tell what is true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Well said. Come, let us go." Saul agrees quickly now, his hesitation overcome by his servant's faith. How often a quieter voice—a servant, a friend—speaks the word that moves us forward. I'm grateful for the faithful people the Lord places beside us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Young maidens going out to draw water—the ordinary rhythm of a city's day. Yet they meet Saul on the ascent, answer his question, redirect him. I think the Lord often speaks through the simplest encounters, through young voices, through those going about their daily tasks without knowing they carry a message.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He is before you." The seer is already there, already waiting—they tell Saul to hurry. I marvel at how the Lord's timing works: Saul seeks, not knowing he is being sought. Samuel is already in place, already prepared. The Lord never leaves his appointed hour unwatched.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samuel blesses the sacrifice before the people eat—his word sets apart what is holy. Even now I see how a faithful life, lived close to God, sanctifies what it touches. Others sense that holiness, know to wait, to listen. What a gift to live so close to the Lord that others feel His presence through us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They arrive at the exact moment: Samuel coming out, Saul coming in. The timing is too perfect for chance. I've learned that the Lord often works this way—orchestrating the small movements until suddenly we find ourselves exactly where we were always meant to be.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord had already told Samuel a day before—"Tomorrow about this time." While Saul was seeking donkeys, the Lord was preparing His servant's heart. This is the beauty of providence: our small moves are held within a larger plan we cannot yet see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have looked upon my people, because their cry has come to me." The Lord hears His people's cry and sends deliverance through an unexpected vessel. Saul is chosen not because he is perfect but because the Lord sees the nation's need. Grace often works this way—meeting our deepest cry through what we never would have chosen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Behold, the man of whom I spoke to you!" Samuel sees Saul and hears the Lord confirm it. I think of all the moments we pass near our future without recognizing it. How wise to walk with those who listen to the Lord—they help us see what our eyes alone would miss.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul still doesn't know—he approaches Samuel in the gateway asking simply where the seer's house is. There is an innocence here, a not-yet-knowing. The Lord moves us into place often long before we understand why we are there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I am the seer." Samuel speaks plainly. Then he opens the door—come eat with me, stay the night, and I will tell you all that is in your heart. What a promise: someone who will speak truth about what lies hidden inside us. The Lord gives us such people sometimes, if we are wise to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Your donkeys who were lost three days ago... have been found." Samuel speaks it as fact, already known to the Lord. Then he speaks Saul's true destiny: "For whom is all that is desirable in Israel?" The small loss is swallowed up in the greater word. The Father knows what we truly seek.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul's response speaks volumes: I am nothing—the smallest tribe, the least family. His humility is real, not false. He does not feel equipped for greatness. How often does the Lord choose those who know their own smallness? It leaves room for Him to work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samuel seats Saul in the place of honor among thirty guests—a public signing of what will come. Those gathered could not know it yet, but they are witnessing the moment a shepherd's son becomes a future king. Sometimes the Lord writes His purposes in plain sight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samuel had set aside a special portion beforehand. Again, the preparation—Samuel was ready, waiting. I think of how the Lord prepares His people, sets apart what is needed before we even arrive. There is a strange comfort in knowing we are expected.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The thigh, the honored portion, placed before Saul. "For the appointed time has it been kept for you." What a phrase—held in readiness for this very hour. In all of Scripture, I find this thread running through: the Lord keeps His gifts ready for those He calls at their appointed time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They come down from the high place and sit together on the housetop. The feasting done, now comes the word. Saul is ready to listen, his heart prepared by what he has seen and eaten. Sometimes the Lord breaks bread with us before He opens our ears to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They rise early—the great word comes at daybreak. Samuel calls Saul to wake, to go outside into the morning air. I picture that moment: Saul stepping into the dawn, not yet knowing his life has already changed, about to be told.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Stand still first, that I may cause you to hear God's message." Readers today hear an echo in these words: the Lord still calls us to stand still, to listen, to make space for His word to reach us. How often we rush ahead when what we most need is to stop and hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
